growth_stage: Vegetative; may also damage reproductive stages
visible_symptoms: Small scratch marks or translucent window-pane-like patches on leaves; small larvae may be present.
follow_up_questions: Are the marks translucent or scratch-like? Can you see small caterpillars? Is the damage on several plants?
recommended_observation: Inspect several affected plants, including the whorl, and note whether larvae or fresh feeding damage are present.
management_options: Use integrated pest management and seek locally validated advice before choosing a control measure.
escalation_conditions: Damage is spreading, many plants are affected, or the farmer is unsure what pest is present.
rights_status: Review reuse terms before redistributing source-derived content
safety_note: Symptoms suggest but do not confirm fall armyworm. Do not recommend a pesticide from text symptoms alone.

visible_symptoms: Larger ragged or elongated holes, shredded leaves, and frass (insect droppings); larvae may hide in the whorl.
affected_plant_part: Leaves; whorl; at reproductive stages, tassels, ears or grains
follow_up_questions: Are there ragged holes? Is there frass in the whorl? Have you seen a caterpillar?
recommended_observation: Look carefully inside the whorl and on damaged leaves; record whether larvae and fresh damage are visible.
management_options: Use integrated pest management and obtain locally validated advice on suitable control options.
escalation_conditions: Heavy or increasing damage, damage to ears, or uncertain identification.
rights_status: Review reuse terms before redistributing source-derived content
safety_note: Do not diagnose solely from holes; other causes can produce similar damage.

scientific_name: Various stem-borer species; species not specified in this record
visible_symptoms: Caterpillar feeding on young plants may cause dead hearts; larvae may later bore into stems.
follow_up_questions: Are central leaves drying or failing to emerge? Can you see holes or signs of boring in the stem?
recommended_observation: Inspect affected shoots and stems for signs of feeding or boring; avoid cutting many plants unless guided by an extension worker.
management_options: KALRO describes integrated options including intercropping/non-host crops, trap crops and biological control; locally verify suitability.
escalation_conditions: Multiple plants show dead hearts or stem-boring symptoms.
safety_note: Dead-heart symptoms are not unique to stem borers.

problem_name: Maize leafhoppers / possible maize streak virus risk
scientific_name: Leafhopper species; KALRO page references maize leafhoppers
visible_symptoms: Small slender hoppers may be present; plants may show chlorotic or yellow streaking.
affected_plant_part: Leaves; whole plant may be affected
follow_up_questions: Are there narrow yellow or white streaks? Have you seen small hopping insects on the plants?
recommended_observation: Inspect leaves for streak patterns and check for small hoppers; record both findings separately.
management_options: KALRO lists field hygiene, early planting and resistant varieties among options; confirm locally relevant guidance.
escalation_conditions: Streaking is widespread or central leaves are dying.
safety_note: Vector presence and virus symptoms need careful interpretation; do not confirm a virus from text alone.

growth_stage: Especially young leaves; dry periods noted by KALRO
visible_symptoms: Small, soft-bodied dark green to bluish-green insects; mottling, stunted growth, dieback or black sooty mould may occur.
follow_up_questions: Can you see clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects? Are leaves mottled or sticky, or is black mould visible?
recommended_observation: Check the undersides of young leaves and note whether beneficial insects such as ladybirds are present.
management_options: KALRO lists predators/parasites and mixed or trap cropping; chemical options should only be considered under approved local guidance.
escalation_conditions: Infestation is increasing or plants show substantial stunting/dieback.
safety_note: Avoid recommending spraying without confirming the pest and assessing severity.

scientific_name: Agrotis spp. noted in KALRO repository material
visible_symptoms: Young seedlings cut off at or near ground level; caterpillars may be found in soil.
follow_up_questions: Are seedlings cut near the ground? Are nearby plants affected? Have you found caterpillars in the soil?
recommended_observation: Inspect the soil around recently cut seedlings and record the number of affected plants.
management_options: Seek extension guidance for locally approved seed or bait control options; avoid improvised chemical use.
escalation_conditions: Seedling loss is spreading or many plants are being cut.
safety_note: Other causes can cut or damage seedlings; confirm before treatment.

scientific_name: Species not specified in this record
visible_symptoms: White or yellow stripes on leaves and leaf sheaths; whole-plant stunting may occur.
follow_up_questions: Are stripes white or yellow and visible on the leaf and sheath? Are affected plants stunted?
recommended_observation: Compare several affected plants and note whether symptoms are striped and whether growth is stunted.
management_options: KALRO lists early planting, crop rotation and resistant varieties; confirm recommendations for the location and season.
escalation_conditions: Several plants show similar symptoms or plants are severely stunted.
safety_note: Do not treat visual symptoms as a confirmed diagnosis.

problem_name: Northern corn leaf blight (Turcicum leaf blight; possible)
scientific_name: Source page uses the common disease name; verify scientific nomenclature with expert
growth_stage: Symptoms may increase as crop develops
visible_symptoms: Lesions may start as chlorotic halos and develop into long cigar-shaped lesions, first often on lower leaves.
follow_up_questions: Are the lesions long and cigar-shaped? Did they start on lower leaves and increase in number?
recommended_observation: Photograph affected leaves and inspect lower and upper leaves for lesion shape and spread.
management_options: KALRO lists resistant varieties, crop rotation and fungicides in early disease stages; any treatment must follow current local guidance.
escalation_conditions: Lesions spread rapidly or large parts of the canopy are affected.
safety_note: Fungicide advice requires expert confirmation and approved product-label guidance.

visible_symptoms: Light-brown leaf spots with darker margins; spots may expand and leaves may dry prematurely.
follow_up_questions: Are spots light brown with darker margins? Are they spreading or joining together?
recommended_observation: Record where spots first appear and whether they are limited by leaf veins; take a clear photo if possible.
management_options: KALRO lists disease-free seed, crop-residue management, crop rotation and tolerant varieties.
escalation_conditions: Spots spread across many leaves or premature drying is increasing.
safety_note: Leaf spots have multiple possible causes; do not diagnose from one symptom.

growth_stage: Often increases after silking according to KALRO page
visible_symptoms: Long narrow lesions may start on lower leaves, become grey, increase in number and merge.
follow_up_questions: Are lesions long and narrow? Are they becoming grey and joining together, starting on lower leaves?
recommended_observation: Inspect lower leaves and note lesion shape, colour and whether lesions are merging.
management_options: KALRO lists field hygiene, tolerant/resistant varieties, early planting and crop rotation.
escalation_conditions: Lesions are spreading rapidly or large portions of leaves are dying.
safety_note: Symptoms may overlap with other leaf blights; expert confirmation recommended.

growth_stage: Often noticeable around tasseling according to KALRO page
visible_symptoms: Raised elongated red-brown to dark-brown pustules may occur on both leaf surfaces and later darken.
affected_plant_part: Leaves, particularly mid and upper canopy
follow_up_questions: Are there raised rust-coloured bumps on either side of the leaf? Are they scattered or clustered?
recommended_observation: Check both sides of several leaves and record the colour and distribution of pustules.
management_options: KALRO lists resistant varieties and cultural practices; fungicide use requires current local expert advice.
escalation_conditions: Pustules are widespread or crop condition is deteriorating.
safety_note: Do not recommend fungicide solely from a text description.

growth_stage: May affect multiple growth stages and plant parts
visible_symptoms: Galls or swollen growths may replace kernels or appear on stalks, leaves or tassels; later galls may rupture and release dark spores.
follow_up_questions: Are there swollen growths or galls? Where on the plant are they? Have any ruptured?
recommended_observation: Record the location of any gall and seek extension confirmation before handling or disposing of affected material.
management_options: KALRO lists field hygiene, resistant varieties and avoiding plant injury.
escalation_conditions: Galls are widespread or the farmer is unsure how to manage affected material.
safety_note: Do not advise consumption or disposal practices without confirming the problem and local guidance.

problem_name: Maize lethal necrosis disease (possible; urgent review)
scientific_name: Viral disease complex; confirm with specialist
visible_symptoms: Chlorotic mottling may start near the base of young leaves in the whorl and extend toward tips; severe cases may include dead hearts, dwarfing and poor grain filling.
affected_plant_part: Young leaves/whorl; whole plant; tassels and ears
follow_up_questions: Is mottling starting in young leaves in the whorl? Are plants stunted or are central leaves dying?
recommended_observation: Record how many plants show symptoms, the field location and whether symptoms are spreading; contact an extension officer promptly.
management_options: KALRO lists integrated management, certified seed, field hygiene, vector/host management and crop rotation.
escalation_conditions: Suspected symptoms are present, especially if spreading across the field.
source_basis: KALRO maize crop protection page; KALRO MLN repository reference
safety_note: Potentially serious condition; AgriMama should escalate rather than give a definitive diagnosis.

visible_symptoms: Narrow white or yellow streaks on leaves; severe symptoms may include dying central leaves or a dead-heart appearance.
follow_up_questions: Are streaks narrow and parallel along the leaf? Are central leaves dying? Have you seen leafhoppers?
recommended_observation: Record the streak pattern, affected plants and whether small leafhoppers are present.
management_options: KALRO lists resistant varieties, early planting and grass-weed management; confirm local suitability.
escalation_conditions: Many plants have streaking or central leaves are dying.
safety_note: Similar symptoms can have other causes; escalate suspected viral disease.

problem_name: Routine maize pest and disease scouting
visible_symptoms: Look for insects, eggs or larvae, leaf damage, spots, streaks, wilting, stunting and changes across the field.
affected_plant_part: Whole plant; inspect leaf surfaces and whorls
follow_up_questions: When did the problem start? How many plants are affected? Is it spreading? What crop stage is the maize at?
recommended_observation: Walk through the field in a zigzag or W-shaped pattern, inspect leaves including undersides, and note affected areas. KALRO's KCEP manual describes weekly scouting as a general practice.
management_options: Use integrated pest and disease management combining monitoring, cultural, biological and other locally approved methods.
escalation_conditions: Symptoms spread, many plants are affected, the crop is deteriorating, or identification remains uncertain.
source_basis: KALRO KCEP Maize Production Training and Extension Manual
rights_status: Review source reuse terms before redistribution
safety_note: Scouting helps collect evidence; it does not itself confirm a diagnosis.
